title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Solitary fibrous tumors (SFTs) are rare mesenchymal neoplasms that can arise virtually anywhere in the body, most often within the thoracic cavity. While many SFTs follow a benign course, a subset exhibits malignant potential with local recurrence or distant metastasis, posing diagnostic and management challenges. Accurate identification requires a multidisciplinary approach that integrates clinical evaluation, advanced imaging, histopathologic assessment, immunohistochemistry, and molecular testing to distinguish SFTs from other spindle cell neoplasms.

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This educational activity provides a comprehensive overview of the epidemiology, molecular pathogenesis, clinical presentation, diagnostic evaluation, and treatment of SFTs. Participants learn to interpret characteristic imaging and immunohistochemical findings, recognize the significance of the NAB2–STAT6 fusion, and apply evidence-based strategies for surgical, radiotherapeutic, and systemic management. The activity also reviews prognostic factors, risk-stratification models, and long-term surveillance recommendations for optimizing patient outcomes. By engaging in this activity, participants strengthen their competence in diagnosing and managing SFTs. Through improved communication, coordinated care, and collaborative decision-making, they can enhance early recognition, ensure effective treatment planning, and ultimately improve the quality of life and prognosis for patients with solitary fibrous tumors.

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Introduction
content: The historical evolution of solitary fibrous tumors (SFTs) dates to the late nineteenth century, when Wagner first described pleural lesions resembling benign mesothelioma in 1870. Klemperer and Rabin clearly delineated the entity in 1931, who reported 5 cases of primary pleural neoplasms arising from submesothelial areolar tissue rather than the mesothelial lining. [1] [2] In 1942, Stout and Murray introduced the term hemangiopericytoma (HPC) to describe a morphologically similar vascular spindle-cell tumor of pericytic origin. [3] In 1951, Stout and Himadi described a series of 8 well-circumscribed pleural tumors, then referred to as solitary (localized) mesothelioma, that are now recognized as SFTs. [4]

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Introduction
content: Initially regarded as separate entities, subsequent morphologic, immunohistochemical, and molecular studies demonstrated that SFTs and HPCs represent morphologic variants within a single fibroblastic spectrum unified by the NAB2-STAT6 gene fusion. This concept, first articulated by Gengler and Guillou, is now reflected in the World Health Organization (WHO) classification, which consolidates SFTs and HPCs into a single clinicopathologic spectrum. [5] Recognition of extrapleural SFTs expanded after the first large series in 1991, establishing that these tumors can arise in virtually any anatomic site, including the meninges, retroperitoneum, abdomen, and extremities. [6]

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Introduction
content: SFTs are rare fibroblastic mesenchymal neoplasms, accounting for approximately 3.7% of visceral and soft-tissue sarcomas. They represent a heterogeneous group of fibroblastic mesenchymal tumors that are typically benign but may rarely exhibit malignant behavior with metastatic potential. Although most follow an indolent course, a subset demonstrates aggressive behavior with local recurrence or distant metastasis. They can arise in a wide range of anatomic sites and typically present as well-circumscribed, slow-growing masses that remain asymptomatic until large enough to compress adjacent structures. [7] [8] [9]

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Introduction
content: Diagnosis can be challenging because of variable histologic patterns and overlap with other spindle-cell tumors. The discovery of the NAB2-STAT6 gene fusion, and its surrogate marker nuclear STAT6 immunostaining, has markedly improved diagnostic precision. Nevertheless, distinguishing SFTs from morphologic mimics remains critical because management and prognosis differ significantly across the spectrum of fibroblastic neoplasms. [6]

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Etiology
content: The exact etiology of SFTs remains uncertain. However, current evidence supports their origin from mesenchymal fibroblastic cells. [10] The defining molecular hallmark is a recurrent fusion of the NAB2 and STAT6 genes on chromosome 12q13, which disrupts NAB2 -mediated repression and leads to aberrant activation of early growth response transcription pathways, driving tumorigenesis. [6] No environmental or occupational exposures have been linked to SFT development. Although hormonal or hereditary factors have been proposed, definitive associations have not been established. [10]

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Epidemiology
content: SFTs have been reported at nearly every anatomic site. The age-adjusted incidence rates are 0.61 per million persons per year for extrameningeal cases and 0.37 per million persons per year for meningeal cases, corresponding to an estimated 1 new case per million individuals annually. [11] The pleura is the most common primary site, accounting for roughly 30% of all SFTs and representing less than 5% of all pleural tumors, with an estimated incidence of 2.8 per 100,000 people. [12]

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Epidemiology
content: Other frequently involved anatomic sites include the meninges (27%), the abdominal cavity (20%), the trunk (10%), the extremities (8%), and the head and neck region (5%). [6] [13] Intracranial SFTs account for approximately 2.5% of meningeal neoplasms and less than 1% of all intracranial tumors. [14] SFTs occur primarily in adults aged 20 to 70, with a peak incidence in the fifth and sixth decades of life, and are rare in children and adolescents. [10] Pleural SFTs tend to present at a somewhat older age (mean, 60.2 years) than meningeal (50.6 years) or extrapleural (50.3 years) forms. [6] There is no clear sex predilection, although a slight male predominance has been reported in certain histologic variants, such as the fat-forming type (male-to-female ratio ≈ 3.2). [2] [13] [2] [15]

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Pathophysiology
content: The pathophysiology of SFTs is not yet fully understood, although current evidence suggests a mesenchymal fibroblastic origin. The defining molecular hallmark is a recurrent fusion of the NAB2 and STAT6 genes on chromosome 12q13, which is considered an early molecular event in the tumorigenesis of SFT. [6] This fusion produces an abnormal transcriptional activator that constitutively activates early growth response target genes, leading to unregulated fibroblastic proliferation and tumorigenesis. [13]

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Pathophysiology
content: While the mechanisms underlying the variable clinical behavior of SFTs remain incompletely defined, no consistent patient-related, environmental, or dietary factors have been implicated in their development or malignant potential. [16] [17] Although most SFTs are biologically indolent, a subset exhibits malignant potential. Aggressive behavior is associated with older age, larger tumor size, hypercellularity, elevated mitotic activity (>4 mitoses per 10 high-power fields or >2 mitoses per mm²), nuclear pleomorphism, necrosis, and infiltrative margins. [18] Tumors lacking these features at presentation may acquire them upon recurrence or metastasis. In extrapleural and meningeal sites, hypercellularity, increased mitotic activity, and nuclear atypia correlate with recurrence or metastasis.

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Pathophysiology
content: SFTs spread primarily via hematogenous dissemination, most commonly to the lungs and, less frequently, the intra-abdominal organs. Lymphatic spread is rare. Extrathoracic SFTs show a slightly higher propensity for metastasis than intrathoracic ones. [19] The 2020 WHO classification designates SFT as an intermediate-grade fibroblastic neoplasm, reflecting its potential for recurrence and rare distant metastasis. Molecular alterations beyond NAB2-STAT6 have been linked to tumor progression, including TP53 and TERT promoter mutations, which correlate with recurrence and metastasis. Recent risk stratification models integrate patient age, mitotic index, tumor size, and degree of necrosis to better predict clinical outcomes and guide management decisions. [11]

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Pathophysiology
content: Paraneoplastic syndromes, though rare, illustrate the systemic effects of SFTs. Hypertrophic osteoarthropathy (HOA), also known as Pierre-Marie-Bamberger syndrome, is observed in fewer than 10% of cases and typically involves pleural SFTs. Patients may present with digital clubbing, hypertrophic skin changes, and arthralgia, with imaging findings consistent with increased periosteal activity. [20] Clubbing may be asymptomatic or associated with pain, typically affecting the distal phalanges. Diagnosis is based on the combination of clubbing and radiographic periostosis, reflecting altered systemic vascularization mediated by overexpression of vascular endothelial growth factor and platelet-derived growth factor.

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Pathophysiology
content: HOA is distinct from Doege-Potter syndrome, another paraneoplastic syndrome characterized by hypoglycemia due to tumor overproduction of insulin-like growth factor type II (IGF-II). The resultant IGF-II-mediated activation of insulin receptors suppresses hepatic gluconeogenesis and increases peripheral glucose uptake, leading to non-islet-cell tumor hypoglycemia. [21] The reported incidence of Doege-Potter syndrome is highly variable, ranging from 0% to 14% across published series, but it is generally considered rare. Both syndromes typically resolve following tumor resection, underscoring the diverse paraneoplastic manifestations of SFTs. [20] [21] [22] [23]

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Histopathology
content: The pathologic diagnosis of SFTs is established through histopathologic evaluation and immunohistochemistry (IHC). Histologically, SFTs exhibit a spectrum of morphological features characterized by ovoid to spindled cells with patternless growth against a collagenous stroma. [6] [24] SFTs characteristically show branching, thin-walled, HPC-like (“staghorn”) vessels. The background stroma may demonstrate focal or diffuse myxoid change. [25]

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Histopathology
content: Classic fibrous SFTs are paucicellular, containing spindle-shaped cells in a densely fibrous stroma. Cellular SFTs, in contrast, are more densely cellular with perivascular fibrosis and gaping blood vessels at the periphery. Cellular tumors resembling HPCs consist of sheets of primitive-appearing rounded cells. Meningeal SFTs tend to be more cellular and display HPC-like morphology. Variants include the fat-forming (lipomatous) SFT, characterized by abundant mature adipocytes, and the giant-cell-rich SFT, featuring multinucleated stromal giant cells arranged around pseudovascular spaces. Dedifferentiation may occur, marked by an abrupt transition to a low- or high-grade sarcomatous component, frequently with spindle-cell or undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma morphology. [6] Rare cases demonstrate epithelioid, squamous, or neuroendocrine differentiation. [25]

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Histopathology
content: Histologic features suggestive of malignancy include moderate-to-severe nuclear atypia, increased cellularity, mitotic activity exceeding four mitoses per 10 high-power fields, infiltrative margins, tumor size ≥10 cm, pleomorphism, hemorrhage, and necrosis. [24] [26] Although these findings are useful indicators of aggressive potential, SFTs may exhibit unpredictable biologic behavior. [27] IHC plays a critical role in confirming the diagnosis of SFTs. Immunophenotypically, SFTs typically express CD34, STAT6, CD99, and Bcl-2, but lack S-100 protein, cytokeratin, and desmin. [6] [18] [28] [18] CD34 is positive in approximately 80% to 95% of cases, but may be diminished or lost in malignant or dedifferentiated variants. CD99 (~94%) and Bcl-2 (~96%) are sensitive, but not specific, markers. [29]

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Histopathology
content: The STAT6 IHC stain has emerged as a valuable surrogate marker for NAB2-STAT6 gene fusion, the defining molecular hallmark of SFT, demonstrating excellent sensitivity and specificity. According to the fifth edition of the WHO Classification of Tumors of the Central Nervous System, SFTs and intracranial HPCs both share IHC features of NAB2 and STAT6 gene fusion, as well as STAT6 overexpression. [14] [30] However, weak STAT6 expression may rarely be observed in other neoplasms, including dedifferentiated liposarcoma, well-differentiated liposarcoma, and deep fibrous histiocytoma, necessitating careful interpretation in the appropriate histologic context. [28]

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Histopathology
content: Additional immunohistochemical and molecular markers may support the diagnosis of SFT. Gene expression profiling has demonstrated overexpression of GRIA2 and aberrant GRIA2 protein expression in SFTs, which may assist in distinguishing SFT from other spindle cell neoplasms. Aldehyde dehydrogenase has also shown diagnostic utility, particularly when combined with STAT6, and may aid in differentiating SFT from morphologic mimics such as meningioma and synovial sarcoma. Multifocal cytokeratin or epithelial membrane antigen expression can occur in a minority of pleural or abdominal SFTs, contributing to diagnostic complexity, whereas S100 protein, desmin, CD32, and h-caldesmon are almost always negative. [6] TP53 IHC expression has also been associated with tumor recurrence and metastasis, reflecting its correlation with malignant transformation rather than diagnostic specificity. [31]

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- History and Physical
content: A thorough history and physical examination are essential in evaluating patients with suspected SFTs. Clinical manifestations depend on the site of origin, but most commonly include pain, a palpable mass, or compression-related symptoms of nearby structures. Tumors in the abdomen or pelvis may present with urinary retention or bowel obstruction. [9]

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- History and Physical
content: History-taking should include the onset and duration of localized symptoms, such as pain, swelling, or changes in bowel or bladder habits, as well as systemic manifestations suggestive of paraneoplastic syndromes. Episodes of hypoglycemia may indicate Doege-Potter syndrome, caused by tumor secretion of IGF-2. [9] Arthralgia, digital clubbing, or HOA may suggest Pierre-Marie-Bamberger syndrome. [32]

content: Past medical history should document prior surgeries, trauma, or radiation exposure to the affected region. title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- History and Physical
content: Physical examination should focus on the suspected tumor site. Palpation may reveal a firm, usually nontender mass. Overlying skin changes, such as erythema or ulceration, and evidence of neurovascular compromise should be noted when the lesion is in a critical anatomic location. A comprehensive systemic examination is recommended to evaluate for metastatic disease or paraneoplastic features. This includes a focused neurologic and respiratory assessment, inspection for digital clubbing, and evaluation for other signs of endocrine or metabolic dysfunction.

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Evaluation -- Laboratory Studies
content: There are no specific laboratory tests diagnostic for SFTs. Routine bloodwork is typically unremarkable. Baseline evaluation often includes a complete blood count, basic metabolic panel, and liver function tests to assess overall fitness for biopsy or surgical intervention. Specific paraneoplastic findings may provide diagnostic clues. Hypoglycemia, when present, can suggest Doege-Potter syndrome, resulting from tumor secretion of incompletely processed IGF-II. In these cases, laboratory findings include low glucose levels, suppressed insulin and C-peptide levels, and elevated IGF-II levels. Clubbing and HOA may occur in Pierre-Marie-Bamberger syndrome, another paraneoplastic manifestation of pleural SFTs.

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Evaluation -- Radiologic Evaluation
content: CT chest with intravenous contrast for all soft tissue tumors ≥5 cm or deep to fascia, to evaluate for pulmonary metastases. MRI of the primary site to define anatomic relationships and surgical margins. CT or MRI of the abdomen and pelvis for retroperitoneal, abdominopelvic, or visceral lesions. Whole-body PET/CT or bone scan only when metastatic disease is suspected.

Whole-body PET/CT or bone scan only when metastatic disease is suspected.

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Evaluation -- Computed Tomography
content: CT is the preferred initial imaging method for most SFTs. These tumors are typically well-defined and hypervascular, with approximately 65% demonstrating avid contrast enhancement. Enhancement is most conspicuous in the arterial and early portal venous phases and may wash out on delayed images. When fibrous stroma predominates, delayed enhancement becomes more marked as contrast diffuses into collagenous tissue. [35]

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Evaluation -- Computed Tomography
content: Heterogeneous enhancement occurs more often in malignant SFTs (reported in 100% of malignant and 60% of benign cases). [36] SFTs typically demonstrate intermediate to high attenuation on unenhanced CT scans due to dense collagen fibers and a rich capillary network. Regions of low attenuation on unenhanced CT commonly correspond to areas of cystic or myxoid degeneration within the tumor, reflecting internal necrosis or hemorrhage in some cases. These features are frequently observed in SFTs and contribute to their heterogeneous enhancement pattern. These radiological findings aid in assessing tumor aggressiveness and guiding treatment decisions. [9]

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Evaluation -- Computed Tomography
content: Intra-abdominal and retroperitoneal SFTs typically appear as well-circumscribed, hypervascular masses with variable cystic or necrotic components. They are generally isodense to adjacent muscle on unenhanced images and typically demonstrate avid, heterogeneous enhancement after contrast administration. Nonenhancing central zones may indicate necrosis or cyst formation. Coarse calcifications can occur in larger or malignant lesions. [37] [38]

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Evaluation -- Computed Tomography
content: Pleural SFTs typically appear as well-circumscribed, homogeneous masses arising from the pleural surface, sometimes demonstrating lobulated contours. [39] [40] On contrast-enhanced CT, they usually exhibit prominent enhancement due to their rich capillary network, whereas areas of cystic or myxoid degeneration appear hypoattenuating. [39] These tumors may displace or invade adjacent thoracic structures and, when pedunculated, can exhibit positional or morphologic changes with respiration. [41] [39] Associated pleural effusion may also be seen on CT imaging. [42] [43] Radiographic features such as large tumor size, pleural effusion, necrosis, and calcification are more suggestive of malignant pleural SFTs. [37] [38]

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Evaluation -- Magnetic Resonance Imaging
content: On MRI, pleural SFTs demonstrate variable appearance due to their mixed fibrous and cystic components. On T1-weighted images, the solid components are typically isointense or mildly hypointense relative to skeletal muscle, reflecting their fibrous composition. However, signal intensity may vary, and some solid regions can appear hypointense. On T2-weighted sequences, the solid components of SFTs demonstrate variable signal intensity, ranging from isointense to hypointense relative to skeletal muscle. In contrast, cystic or necrotic areas appear hyperintense, reflecting their fluid content. Following gadolinium administration, SFTs usually exhibit strong, heterogeneous enhancement, reflecting their vascular stroma. The enhancement pattern mirrors that seen on CT imaging and helps distinguish SFTs from other pleural or soft-tissue lesions. MRI also helps identify necrosis, hemorrhage, and cystic degeneration when present. [11] [35]

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Evaluation -- 18F-FDG-PET/CT
content: On 18F-FDG-PET/CT, data describing SFTs are limited. Results from one study showed that benign SFTs demonstrated low-grade FDG uptake, whereas malignant lesions showed intense, homogeneous hypermetabolism. [36] However, results from another study of 17 pathologically confirmed cases found that 18F-FDG PET/CT did not reliably distinguish indolent (typical) from aggressive (malignant) SFTs, suggesting a limited role in differentiating malignant pleural SFTs from benign counterparts. [44] PET/CT is most useful in evaluating suspected metastasis or recurrence, as metastatic SFTs may demonstrate increased FDG uptake in lymph nodes, bone, or distant soft tissues. This modality can also be employed to monitor treatment response in patients receiving chemotherapy, radiation therapy, or targeted agents, as changes in metabolic activity over time may help assess therapeutic efficacy and guide management.

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Evaluation -- Ultrasound
content: Ultrasound may be used in select cases depending on tumor location. Although not a primary imaging modality for pleural SFTs, it can aid in evaluating extrapleural or superficial lesions. In a reported case of a breast SFT in a 73-year-old man with a 12-month history of a palpable mass and bilateral gynecomastia, ultrasound demonstrated an oval, well-circumscribed, hypoechoic lesion with internal hypervascularity. [24]

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Evaluation -- Tissue Diagnosis and Biopsy Techniques
content: SFT may be suspected based on imaging and clinical features; however, a definitive diagnosis requires histologic tissue confirmation. When imaging studies reveal a soft tissue mass suggestive of SFT, biopsy is typically recommended to obtain tissue for histopathologic and IHC evaluation. A pretreatment biopsy is ideal for establishing the diagnosis and assessing features of malignancy.

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Evaluation -- Tissue Diagnosis and Biopsy Techniques
content: Core needle biopsy preserves the cytologic architecture of the lesion and should be performed by a clinician experienced in soft tissue mass biopsy techniques. Core biopsies are often adequate to establish the diagnosis of SFT but may be limited in demonstrating histologic features associated with aggressive behavior. Repeat biopsy can be considered if the initial sample is nondiagnostic or insufficient. Depending on the tumor’s location, image-guided biopsy may enhance accuracy. [10]

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Evaluation -- Tissue Diagnosis and Biopsy Techniques
content: Fine-needle aspiration (FNA) typically yields inadequate tissue for a definitive diagnosis. Unlike core needle biopsy, FNA does not preserve tissue architecture, limiting its diagnostic yield; however, it remains technically less demanding and may be used in select circumstances. Open incisional or excisional biopsy plays a crucial role in the definitive diagnosis and workup of SFTs. Incisional biopsy involves sampling a portion of the tumor, whereas excisional biopsy entails complete resection. The choice depends on tumor size, location, proximity to critical structures, and suspicion for malignancy.

content: Case reports have documented successful diagnoses of SFTs through open or excisional approaches in various anatomic sites, including the pancreas (confirmed following total pancreatectomy); the mesojejunum (after resection of a left abdominal mass with partial omentectomy); the penis (following en bloc excision for a large soft tissue mass); and the retroperitoneum (after radical resection with nephrectomy, adrenalectomy, and partial hepatectomy). title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Evaluation -- Histopathologic, Immunohistochemical, and Molecular Evaluation
content: Excised tissue samples are examined histologically to assess cellular composition, architectural pattern, and cytologic features characteristic of SFTs. Histopathologic evaluation confirms the diagnosis by identifying the typical spindle-shaped cells, patternless or storiform growth pattern, and branching “staghorn” vasculature. IHC staining demonstrates positivity for CD34, STAT6, and Bcl-2, which are characteristic of SFTs. Some pleural and abdominal SFTs may show multifocal cytokeratin expression. In contrast, focal expression of alpha smooth muscle actin (ASMA), beta-catenin, glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), or neuron-specific enolase (NSE) may also occur. Conversely, h-caldesmon, desmin, CD31, and S100 are almost always negative. [6] TP53 immunohistochemical expression has been observed in malignant cases. [31]

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Evaluation -- Histopathologic, Immunohistochemical, and Molecular Evaluation
content: Molecular testing can detect the pathognomonic NAB2–STAT6 gene fusion, providing further diagnostic specificity. In addition to confirming the diagnosis, histopathologic evaluation provides information regarding tumor subtype and grade, which can guide treatment decisions and prognostic assessment. Overall, the diagnostic workup of SFTs requires a multidisciplinary approach integrating clinical assessment, imaging studies, biopsy with histopathologic and molecular evaluation, and staging to determine disease extent. This comprehensive evaluation is essential for guiding appropriate management and optimizing patient outcomes.

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Treatment / Management
content: Due to the rarity of SFTs and the absence of large prospective clinical trials, standardized treatment guidelines have not been established. Complete surgical resection remains the cornerstone and most effective therapy for localized disease. The roles of radiotherapy, cytotoxic chemotherapy, and targeted agents continue to evolve, and management should be tailored through a multidisciplinary approach. [6] [11] [35]

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Treatment / Management -- Surgery
content: Thoracic SFTs These tumors commonly arise from the visceral pleura and are often pedunculated. Surgical resection typically involves excision of adherent lung parenchyma; for parietal pleural or pulmonary lesions, procedures such as isolated pleural resection, chest wall resection, or pulmonary wedge resection may be required. [26] [46] Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery is increasingly used for smaller tumors (<10 cm). [47] Preoperative angiography can delineate feeding vessels, allowing embolization or thoracoscopic ligation to minimize blood loss. Embolization is particularly effective in reducing intraoperative bleeding for sessile lesions. [48]

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Treatment / Management -- Surgery
content: Abdominal SFTs Most abdominal SFTs occur in the retroperitoneum, with fewer in the pelvis. The goal is complete excision with negative margins while preserving adjacent organs when feasible. In one study, both en bloc and piecemeal resections were acceptable approaches, with no significant difference in 5-year progression-free survival between the groups (63.5%; P = 0.97). Piecemeal resection may be particularly appropriate for sacral or pelvic tumors, where preservation of sacral nerves can help maintain postoperative function. Preoperative embolization may also be considered in select retroperitoneal cases to reduce intraoperative blood loss, as illustrated by a case reporting approximately 17 L of blood loss during resection. [9] Long-term follow-up is essential, as recurrence and metastasis often occur late in the disease course. [11] [49]

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Treatment / Management -- Surgery
content: Meningeal SFTs These tumors typically attach to the dura mater and are intracranial, involving sites such as the tentorium, frontal convexity, cerebellopontine angle, ventricles, falx cerebri, or posterior fossa. Complete resection has been shown to improve prognosis, although defining clear margins can be challenging due to tumor fragmentation. Adjuvant radiotherapy is frequently recommended to achieve locoregional control.

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Treatment / Management -- Surgery
content: Extremity SFTs Surgical management of SFTs in the extremities follows standard principles applied to soft tissue sarcomas. Among reported cases of extremity SFTs, the thigh is the most frequently described site of involvement. [50] These tumors typically present as well-circumscribed masses arising along fascial planes. Although SFTs are often highly vascularized, reports describing significant intraoperative bleeding or the role of preoperative embolization in extremity lesions are limited. Complete surgical excision with negative margins remains the treatment of choice.

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Treatment / Management -- Radiation Therapy
content: No prospective data support neoadjuvant or adjuvant radiotherapy. Adjuvant radiation may improve locoregional control, particularly for tumors with high-risk histologic features, positive margins, or recurrent disease. [6] [9] [51] In locally recurrent pleural SFTs, radiotherapy is often administered after resection of recurrent tumors. For meningeal SFTs, retrospective analyses demonstrate improved local control with adjuvant radiation. [52] Neoadjuvant radiotherapy may be considered for large or anatomically complex tumors to facilitate complete resection. Radiation may also be used palliatively for symptom control in metastatic disease. [53] Treatment should be individualized and guided by a multidisciplinary team.

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Treatment / Management -- Chemotherapy
content: Cytotoxic chemotherapy is generally reserved for advanced or metastatic SFTs. Evidence from retrospective series suggests modest efficacy. Anthracycline-based regimens, often combined with ifosfamide, are the most studied, achieving overall response rates of 10% to 20% and median progression-free survival (PFS) of 3 to 5 months. Dedifferentiated SFTs (DD-SFT) may have somewhat longer PFS than malignant SFTs with these regimens. [11]

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Treatment / Management -- Chemotherapy
content: Other agents, such as dacarbazine (DTIC) and temozolomide, have demonstrated activity, with reported response rates of 38% to 50% and median PFS exceeding 6 months. [11] In a study using patient-derived xenograft models of DD-SFT, the combination of doxorubicin and DTIC produced marked tumor inhibition (>80%) and achieved clinical responses in 6 of 12 patients, with a median PFS of 6 months in malignant SFT and 10 months in DD-SFT. [54] Temozolomide combined with bevacizumab has shown promising activity in retrospective analyses. [55] [56]

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Treatment / Management -- Chemotherapy
content: Trabectedin, a marine-derived alkaloid approved for pretreated metastatic soft-tissue sarcomas, has demonstrated activity in SFTs, particularly in translocation-related subtypes. Preclinical SFT models have shown sensitivity to trabectedin, and retrospective series have reported PFS ranging from 2.3 to 11.6 months. [11] In a multicenter phase 1/2 trial of trabectedin combined with low-dose radiotherapy in metastatic soft-tissue sarcomas, the overall response rate reached 72% and the median PFS was 9.9 months, suggesting a potential synergistic effect between trabectedin and radiotherapy. [57]

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Treatment / Management -- Chemotherapy
content: Eribulin, a microtubule inhibitor used for liposarcomas, has shown preclinical and early clinical activity in SFTs. In a phase 2 study of patients with previously treated soft tissue sarcomas, eribulin achieved a 12-week progression-free rate of 51%, and a median PFS of 4.1 months overall, with a manageable safety profile. [11] [58] While anthracycline-based therapy remains the standard of care for DD-SFT, other agents, including DTIC, temozolomide, trabectedin, and eribulin, are reasonable options or trial candidates. Further clinical studies are needed to define optimal regimens.

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Treatment / Management -- Targeted and Antiangiogenic Therapies
content: Recent advances have highlighted the antiangiogenic and multitargeted tyrosine kinase inhibitor activity in SFTs. The combination of temozolomide and bevacizumab, a recombinant monoclonal antibody targeting vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), provided some of the first clinical evidence supporting the role of antiangiogenic therapy in SFTs. In a retrospective series of 14 patients with locally advanced or metastatic hemangiopericytoma/SFT, tumor response was assessed using the Choi criteria on CT. This method incorporates both tumor size and density to evaluate treatment response. The regimen achieved a 79% response rate (per Choi criteria) and a median PFS of 9.7 months (6-month PFS 78.6%), with myelosuppression as the most common adverse event. [55]

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Treatment / Management -- Targeted and Antiangiogenic Therapies
content: Sunitinib, a multityrosine kinase inhibitor targeting VEGFR and PDGFR, has demonstrated efficacy in retrospective series of patients with advanced SFT. In 1 study of 35 patients, sunitinib achieved a median PFS of 6 months, with better responses observed in malignant SFTs than in DD-SFTs. [59] Sorafenib, a multikinase inhibitor targeting VEGF and platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) receptors, has shown potential activity in advanced solitary fibrous tumors. In a phase II French Sarcoma Group study, 2 of 5 patients with progressive malignant SFT achieved prolonged disease stabilization for approximately 9 months, with a median overall survival of 19.7 months. The treatment was well tolerated, with hand–foot syndrome being the most common grade 3 adverse event. [60]

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Treatment / Management -- Targeted and Antiangiogenic Therapies
content: Pazopanib, an oral small-molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitor targeting VEGF and PDGF receptors, has shown meaningful activity in advanced SFTs. [61] In a retrospective study, pazopanib achieved a 46% partial response rate with a median PFS of 4.7 months. The multicenter phase 2 GEIS-32 trial demonstrated a 58% partial response rate by Choi criteria and 9% by Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST), with a median PFS of 9.8 months (95% CI, 7.2–12.3), confirming efficacy across aggressive and nonaggressive SFT subgroups. [11] [62]

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Treatment / Management -- Targeted and Antiangiogenic Therapies
content: Axitinib, an oral multi-tyrosine kinase inhibitor that actively targets KIT, VEGF receptors, and PDGF receptors, has demonstrated activity in advanced SFTs. Interestingly, partial responses were observed in 44% of patients treated with other antiangiogenic agents, supporting the potential benefit of sequential antiangiogenic therapy. No responses were seen in DD-SFTs, consistent with findings from other targeted studies. [11]

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Surgical Oncology
content: Surgery remains the cornerstone of curative treatment for SFTs. The primary goal is complete resection with negative margins (R0 resection), which is associated with improved local control and long-term survival. The surgical approach depends on tumor location, size, and involvement of adjacent structures. [11] [66]

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Surgical Oncology
content: For thoracic SFTs, most arise from the visceral or parietal pleura and are often pedunculated. Resection typically involves excision of the tumor and a portion of the pleura, with lobectomy or wedge resection performed when the lung parenchyma is invaded. Minimally invasive approaches such as video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery are increasingly used for smaller, well-circumscribed lesions (<10 cm), offering reduced morbidity and faster recovery compared with open thoracotomy. [47] [66] Preoperative angiography and embolization can be considered for highly vascular or sessile tumors to reduce intraoperative bleeding. [48]

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Radiation Oncology
content: The role of radiation therapy in SFTs remains adjunctive and individualized. Although no prospective trials exist, retrospective data support its use for locoregional control, especially in patients with positive margins, recurrent disease, or high-risk histologic features. [6] Adjuvant radiotherapy is most often considered following incomplete resection (R1 or R2 margins) or in tumors with malignant or dedifferentiated histology. For meningeal SFTs, postoperative radiotherapy has been associated with improved local control and delayed recurrence. [52]

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Medical Oncology
content: Systemic therapy for SFTs is primarily indicated for advanced, unresectable, or metastatic disease, as localized tumors are best managed surgically. No standardized chemotherapy regimen has demonstrated consistent efficacy, but several cytotoxic and targeted agents have shown activity in retrospective studies and clinical trials.

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Medical Oncology -- Cytotoxic Chemotherapy
content: Traditional anthracycline-based regimens, often combined with ifosfamide, remain the most frequently used first-line cytotoxic approach for advanced SFTs. Reported response rates range from 10% to 20%, with a median PFS of approximately 3 to 5 months. DTIC and temozolomide have demonstrated higher response rates (38%–50%) and median PFS exceeding 6 months, particularly when combined with bevacizumab, a VEGF-targeted agent. Trabectedin, approved for previously treated soft tissue sarcomas, has shown clinical benefit in SFTs, especially in translocation-related and dedifferentiated subtypes, with a reported median PFS of 9 to 10 months. [11] Eribulin, a microtubule inhibitor used in liposarcomas, has also shown activity in preclinical models and early clinical studies. [54]

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Staging
content: The 2013 WHO Classification of soft tissue sarcomas represented a significant advancement in differentiating sarcoma subtypes and categorized SFTs as fibroblastic/myofibroblastic neoplasms. Consequently, the staging of SFTs follows the general principles applied to soft tissue sarcomas. [67] The American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) TNM staging system is the primary framework used for soft tissue sarcomas, evaluating the primary tumor (T), regional lymph nodes (N), and distant metastases (M). However, SFTs demonstrate unique biological behavior that may not fully align with conventional sarcoma staging models. [10]

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Staging -- TNM Staging
content: T: Primary tumor Assesses tumor size, depth, and involvement of adjacent structures. SFTs vary widely in size and may extend into nearby tissues or organs, influencing the T category. Larger or deeply seated tumors are more likely to be malignant. N: Regional lymph nodes Lymph node metastasis is rare, so nodal staging is generally not applicable, and lymphadenectomy is not routinely indicated unless clinically suspected. M: Distant metastasis Although uncommon, metastases can occur, most often to the lungs, liver, bones, or other soft tissues. The presence of metastasis (M1) indicates stage IV disease according to the AJCC staging system.

SFTs are classified as benign or malignant based on cellularity, mitotic activity, nuclear atypia, necrosis, and differentiation. [10] Malignant SFTs carry a higher risk of recurrence and metastasis compared with benign lesions.

The Demicco risk model, among the most validated, incorporates patient age, tumor size, mitotic rate, and necrosis to categorize tumors into low-, intermediate-, or high-risk groups for metastasis. [68] Staging and prognosis assessment require a multidisciplinary approach involving pathologists, radiologists, oncologists, and surgeons to determine disease extent and guide individualized treatment planning.

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Prognosis
content: SFTs demonstrate a broad spectrum of clinical behavior. Most are indolent or locally aggressive, while a subset exhibits malignant potential. Predicting tumor behavior remains challenging, as histologically benign lesions may recur, and some tumors with malignant histologic features can behave indolently. Overall survival for SFTs is generally favorable compared with other sarcomas. In a study of extrathoracic SFTs, the median overall survival ranged from 59 to 94 months, with 5-year and 10-year survival rates of 89% and 73%, respectively. [6] Tumor location is a significant prognostic determinant. Extrathoracic lesions, particularly those arising in the meninges, pelvis, retroperitoneum, or mediastinum, are associated with higher recurrence risk and worse outcomes compared with thoracic SFTs. Meningeal SFTs often exhibit increased cellularity and mitotic activity, contributing to their more aggressive clinical course.

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Prognosis
content: Adverse prognostic factors include positive resection margins, tumor size greater than 10 cm, mitotic activity of 4 or more per 10 high-power fields, or 2 or more mitoses per 2 mm 2 , necrosis, nuclear pleomorphism, and hypercellularity. The presence of malignant or dedifferentiated components also portends a higher risk of recurrence or metastasis. [6] [10] The Demicco risk model incorporates patient age, tumor size, mitotic activity, and necrosis to stratify SFTs into low-, intermediate-, and high-risk categories for metastasis. This system helps predict outcomes and guide postoperative surveillance. [16] [68] Even after complete surgical excision with negative margins, local recurrence or distant metastasis may occur, underscoring the need for long-term follow-up.

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Postoperative and Rehabilitation Care
content: Following surgical resection, patients with SFTs should undergo routine follow-up to detect early local or distant recurrence. Local recurrence has been reported in approximately 7% to 8% of cases after surgical resection, although the true recurrence rate may be higher since recurrences have been documented up to 17 years postoperatively. Although no standardized surveillance guidelines exist due to the rarity of SFTs, ongoing oncologic monitoring is widely recommended. [6] [10] [6] [69]

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Postoperative and Rehabilitation Care
content: A practical surveillance approach, adapted from soft tissue sarcoma guidelines, includes imaging of the primary site every 3 to 4 months during the first 2 to 3 years, then every 6 months until year 5, and annually thereafter. [70] After 5 years, imaging intervals may be extended, as late local recurrence is uncommon. [71] Additional imaging should be symptom-directed. Surveillance should be individualized based on tumor location, histologic risk, and clinical presentation. Since SFTs can recur many years after initial resection, long-term or lifetime follow-up may be warranted in selected patients, particularly those with malignant or high-risk features. [10]

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Patient education and awareness are essential in the early detection, management, and long-term follow-up of SFTs. Because SFTs can occur at various anatomic sites and often present incidentally, educating healthcare providers and patients about their potential manifestations is key to timely diagnosis and treatment. Patients should be informed about common presenting symptoms, such as a slowly enlarging, painless mass or pressure-related symptoms from tumor compression. Emphasizing the importance of prompt medical evaluation for new or unexplained soft-tissue masses can facilitate earlier diagnosis and improved outcomes.

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Education should also address the diagnostic and treatment process, including the roles of imaging and biopsy in confirming the diagnosis and guiding management. Patients should understand that complete surgical resection is the primary treatment, with adjuvant therapy considered in select cases. Following treatment, patients must be counseled on the need for regular surveillance imaging and follow-up visits, as SFTs can recur even many years after resection. Reinforcing adherence to scheduled follow-up can enable early detection of recurrence or metastasis and improve long-term outcomes.

content: Providing access to psychosocial and support resources, including counseling services and patient advocacy groups, can help patients and families cope with the emotional impact of diagnosis and treatment. Encouraging healthy lifestyle practices, such as balanced nutrition, regular physical activity, and avoiding tobacco and excessive alcohol, can support overall well-being and recovery. Clinicians should also inform eligible patients about clinical trial opportunities investigating targeted or novel therapies for advanced or recurrent SFTs. By providing effective patient education and consistent follow-up, clinicians can empower patients to participate in their care and improve long-term outcomes actively.

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: The management of SFTs requires close collaboration among an interprofessional team to ensure accurate diagnosis, effective treatment, and long-term surveillance. Because SFTs present across a broad anatomic and biologic spectrum, optimal outcomes depend on coordinated care among physicians, advanced practitioners, nurses, pharmacists, and allied health professionals. Physicians and advanced clinicians play a central role in diagnosis through comprehensive clinical evaluation, interpretation of imaging, and use of immunohistochemical and molecular studies such as STAT6 and NAB2–STAT6 fusion testing. Pathologists provide critical expertise in confirming the diagnosis and assessing histologic features that inform prognosis and risk stratification. Surgeons play a crucial role in achieving complete resection with negative margins, which remains the cornerstone of curative treatment, and oncologists guide decisions on adjuvant or systemic therapy for advanced or recurrent disease.

title: Solitary Fibrous Tumors -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Interprofessional collaboration, including participation in multidisciplinary tumor board discussions, is essential to coordinate individualized management plans, align treatment strategies with patient goals, and prevent delays in diagnosis and treatment. Nurses play a pivotal role in coordinating perioperative and long-term care, providing patient education, managing symptoms, monitoring for postoperative or treatment-related complications, and facilitating adherence to follow-up schedules. Pharmacists contribute critical expertise by ensuring safe and effective medication use, reviewing complex drug regimens for interactions, and counseling patients on potential side effects and adherence strategies. Social workers, physical and occupational therapists, and other allied health professionals provide psychosocial support, assist with rehabilitation and recovery, and help patients maintain function and quality of life during and after treatment. By maintaining open communication, conducting regular case reviews, and coordinating follow-up, the healthcare team can provide comprehensive, patient-centered care that improves safety, enhances outcomes, and supports long-term disease surveillance.
